scenes.heading: Collecting and classifying data
scenes.sub: Is your answer a label, a count or a measurement?
scenes.say: Every survey, sports score and weather report starts with data. But not all data is the same type, and the type decides what you can do with it. Let's sort it out.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Sorting washing into piles: socks, shirts, towels
scenes.science: Categorical data sorts answers into labelled groups
scenes.breaks: Some data looks like a number but is really a label, like a postcode or a jersey number.
scenes.say: Think about sorting washing. Socks go in one pile, shirts in another. Those piles are like categorical data: answers that are labels. But you might also weigh the load or time how long it takes to dry. Those are numbers, so that's numerical data. Careful though: a postcode looks like a number, but it's really a label.

scenes.heading: Two main types

left.title: Categorical
points: Ordinal if there's an order: S, M, L

scenes.say: Categorical data puts answers into groups, like favourite fruit or eye colour. If the groups have an order, like small, medium and large, it's called ordinal. Numerical data is counts or measurements, like number of pets or height. A quick test: if an average makes sense, it's numerical.

scenes.heading: Counted or measured?
scenes.say: Numerical data splits again. Discrete data is counted, like pets or goals. You can't have two point four pets. Continuous data is measured, like height, mass or time, and can be any value in a range. Remember: count it, it's discrete. Measure it, it's continuous.

scenes.heading: Collecting data fairly
points: Population: the whole group you care about
Sample: the part you actually ask
scenes.say: The population is the whole group you want to know about. The sample is the smaller group you actually ask. A good sample is like a mini version of the population. Asking only the soccer team about favourite sports gives a biased result. And keep your questions neutral and clear.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: 15 students: how many pets? 0,2,1,1,3,0,1,2,1,0,4,1,2,0,1. How many have 2 or more?
scenes.say: Fifteen students said how many pets they have. Tally each value: four zeros, six ones, three twos, one three and one four. Check the total is fifteen. Two or more means two, three or four pets. Three plus one plus one gives five students.
scenes.caption: Fifteen students said how many pets they have. Tally each value: four 0s, six 1s, three 2s, one 3 and one 4. Check the total is 15. 2 or more means 2, 3 or 4 pets. 3 + 1 + 1 gives 5 students.

points: Count it: discrete. Measure it: continuous
Samples should be random and representative
Frequency tables: list every value, check total
scenes.say: Quick recap. Categorical data is labels, numerical data is counts or measurements. Count it, it's discrete. Measure it, it's continuous. Use a fair, mixed sample, and always check your frequency table adds up. Now try the practice questions!
